title: The Currency Gap Every Australian Exporter Feels Between the Quote and the Payment
excerpt: An exporter's margin is set the day a price is quoted, but it is only confirmed the day payment lands. Here is why that gap matters more than most export businesses plan for.
content:
For a business selling into overseas markets, the moment that actually decides the deal's margin is not the moment the contract is signed. It is the moment the foreign currency payment is converted back into Australian dollars, which can sit weeks or months after the invoice went out.

Most Australian exporters price a job, a shipment or a contract using the exchange rate they can see on the day of the quote. That rate feels solid at the time. It is not fixed. Between quote day and the day the funds actually land and convert, the Australian dollar can move meaningfully against the US dollar, the euro, or whichever currency the deal is denominated in, and the business only finds out which way once the bank statement shows the converted figure.

This is not a treasury problem tucked away from the rest of the business. It is a margin problem hiding inside a currency problem, and it shows up as a quarter that looked strong on the order book and thinner than expected on the P&L.

Why the Margin You Quoted Isn't the Margin You Bank

A quote built at 0.66 against the US dollar and settled at 0.63 delivers meaningfully more Australian dollars than the number in the original pricing model. The reverse is just as true, and it is the direction that causes the damage. A margin that looked comfortable on the day of the quote can be thin or gone entirely by the time the money is actually in the account, without a single thing going wrong operationally.

The businesses that feel this hardest are the ones pricing tightly to stay competitive against other exporters and importers pricing in the same currency. A small movement against a five or ten per cent margin is not a rounding error. It is the difference between a profitable contract and a break-even one, and the business rarely sees it coming because the exposure sits between two dates that are easy to lose sight of once the shipment is out the door.

The Length of the Exposure Window Is the Real Risk

The size of the currency risk is not really about how far the rate moves. It is about how long the money is exposed to movement at all. A deal quoted, invoiced and paid within a week carries relatively little exposure. A deal quoted at the start of a production run, shipped eight weeks later, and paid on 60 or 90 day terms after that carries a currency exposure window that can stretch past four months, which is a long time for a rate to sit unmanaged.

Mapping that window for each major customer or contract, rather than thinking about currency risk as one general business worry, is what turns an abstract concern into something manageable. Businesses shipping out of Brisbane and other east coast ports are exposed to exactly the same lag regardless of the size of the operation. The exposure window does not care whether the business turns over two million dollars or twenty.

A Hedging Policy Is Not Just for Large Exporters

Forward contracts, which lock in a conversion rate ahead of time for a set amount and date, are often assumed to be the domain of large corporates with dedicated treasury teams. In practice, a modest exporter with a handful of large overseas contracts a year has more to gain from locking in certainty than a business is often given credit for. The tool matters less than the decision to have a policy at all, applied consistently rather than only when the rate happens to look favourable.

A genuine FX and treasury policy sets out which proportion of expected foreign currency receipts gets hedged, which provider the business uses, and how often the position gets reviewed. Without that structure in place, currency decisions tend to get made ad hoc, under time pressure, by whoever is looking at the bank account that week, which is a pattern that rarely produces the best outcome.

Building FX Into the Margin Conversation, Not Just the Treasury Conversation

The businesses that manage this well do not treat currency risk as separate from pricing. They build an assumed exchange rate buffer into the quote itself, they track exposure by customer and by contract rather than as one lump balance sheet figure, and they fold expected currency timing into the same cash flow forecasting rhythm they use for everything else. For businesses running both the commercial and the currency side without a dedicated finance function, this is exactly where an ongoing fractional CFO partner earns its keep, sitting across pricing, cash flow and treasury at once rather than leaving currency exposure as a conversation that only happens after the rate has already moved.

The exchange rate on quote day was never a promise. Treating it as one, even unintentionally, is what turns a genuinely profitable contract into a disappointing one. The fix is not predicting where the dollar goes. It is building a policy that means the business is protected regardless of which way it moves.

faqs.q: Why does an exporter's profit margin change between quoting and getting paid?
faqs.a: A quote is priced using the exchange rate on the day it is given, but the deal is not actually converted into Australian dollars until payment lands, which can be weeks or months later. Whatever the exchange rate does in between changes how many Australian dollars the business actually receives, even though the invoice amount in the foreign currency never changed. The margin quoted and the margin banked are rarely exactly the same number.

faqs.q: What is a hedging policy and does a small export business need one?
faqs.a: A hedging policy sets out how much of the business's expected foreign currency income gets locked in at a known exchange rate ahead of time, typically through a forward contract, and how consistently that decision gets applied. It is not only for large corporates. Any exporter with meaningful overseas contracts and thin margins benefits from certainty over guessing, and a proper FX and treasury review is where that policy gets built.

faqs.q: How long is the currency exposure window between invoicing and payment for exporters?
faqs.a: It depends on the production, shipping and payment terms of each contract, but it is often longer than businesses assume once every stage is added together. A deal quoted at the start of a production run, shipped weeks later, and paid on 60 or 90 day terms can carry several months of currency exposure from the original quote to the final converted payment.

faqs.q: Should a small Australian exporter use forward contracts to manage currency risk?
faqs.a: Forward contracts let a business lock in today's exchange rate for a payment expected in the future, removing the guesswork from that portion of revenue. For exporters pricing tightly against overseas competitors, that certainty is often worth more than the chance of a favourable rate movement. The right proportion to hedge depends on margin, contract size and how much uncertainty the business can absorb.

faqs.q: Can a fractional CFO help set up FX and treasury processes for an export business?
faqs.a: Yes. Currency exposure rarely sits neatly inside one function, it touches pricing, cash flow forecasting and banking relationships at once, which is exactly the gap an ongoing fractional CFO partner is built to cover. Rather than treating FX as a one-off decision, the role is to keep pricing, treasury and forecasting working from the same assumptions as the exchange rate moves.

faqs.q: How do I build currency risk into my business's cash flow forecasting?
faqs.a: Start by mapping expected foreign currency receipts against their likely conversion dates, then apply a conservative exchange rate assumption rather than the current spot rate, so the forecast is not quietly relying on a favourable movement to work. Folding that into the same cash flow forecasting rhythm used for the rest of the business keeps currency risk visible instead of separate.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a favourable and unfavourable FX movement for exporters?
faqs.a: A favourable movement means the Australian dollar has weakened against the currency the business is paid in since the quote was given, so the same foreign currency amount converts into more Australian dollars than expected. An unfavourable movement is the reverse, and it is the one that erodes margin quietly, often only becoming visible once the payment has already landed and converted.
